Therefore, the gods are the principles of all species: there follow them those gods whose prince is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence/substance</gloss>. These sensible <note>perceived by the physical senses</note> beings are of both origins and are similar to them, for they complete all things through sensible nature, each one illuminating its own work through another. Of the heavens, or whatever is understood by that name, the <term>ousiarchēs</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss> is Jupiter. For through the heaven, Jupiter offers life to all. The <term>ousiarchēs</term> of the sun is light; for the goodness of light is infused into us through the orb of the sun. Of the thirty-six stars always fixed in the same place (whose name is Horoscopes), their <term>ousiarchēs</term> or prince is he whom they call <term>Pantomorphon</term> <gloss>all-formed</gloss> or Omniform. He, through diverse species, makes diverse forms. The seven spheres, which are called erratic <note>wandering/planetary</note>, have <term>ousiarchas</term> <gloss>rulers of essence</gloss>, that is, their own princes, which they call fortune, <term>heimarmenēs</term> <gloss>fate/destiny</gloss>, by which all things are changed, with the firmest stability of the law of nature and varied by sempiternal agitation. Truly, the air is the instrument, or machine, of all things through which all things are made. Moreover, this is the second <term>ousiarches</term>. Mortal things are for mortals, and things similar to these exist. Since these things are thus, moving from the bottom to the highest point, all things naturally pertaining to themselves are so connected that mortal things are annexed to mortals, and sensible things to sensible things; yet the sum of governance obeys that highest Lord, so that it is not many, or rather, it is one. For since all things depend upon one, and flow down from him rather than from anything else, when they are at a distance they are seen and believed to be many and divided. But when united, they are one, or rather two: whence all things are made and by whom they are made. That is, from the matter of which they are made, and from His will, by whose nod other things are effected. ASCLEPIUS: What is this reason again, O Trismegistus?
